§5.6 Ignoring and Rejecting

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

layout-ignoring-and-rejecting · rule layout blocks

✅ Normative

A visible region MAY be left out of the output only on the narrow grounds listed below, and a page MAY be declared unrepresentable only when the problem is the page itself. Content that is merely difficult to read MUST NOT be left out on either ground.

Two exclusions, for two different situations. Both are narrow. Visibility is determined by The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1, including hidden text, microscopic text and imperceptible contrast. A visibly present but unreadable text span is represented as [illegible]; it is not an invisible source object.

Excluding one region

A bounded region of an otherwise sound page MAY be left out of the output — no element, no box — only when it is:

  • a scan artifact;
  • an invisible source object;
  • damaged content;
  • an irreconcilable source error;
  • an element explicitly out of scope;
  • a genuinely unresolved ambiguity.

Ordinary logos, page numbers, and content that is difficult but readable MUST NOT be excluded. That is the requirement that matters. Exclusion is not a way past a hard page: a dense figure, an awkward multi-column spread and a badly kerned table are all representable, just slower. Excluding them turns a slow page into missing data, silently — the never drop failure.

An unrepresentable page

A page MAY be declared unrepresentable, and left out of evaluation rather than represented in part, only when it is corrupt, badly cropped, mismatched to its document, unusable, or cannot be represented unambiguously. An unrepresentable page MUST NOT be given a partial or guessed rendering.

Choosing between them

The test is scope. One bad region on an otherwise sound page: that region is excluded and the rest of the page represented. A page where the problem is the page: the page is declared unrepresentable. Excluding twenty regions to rescue a broken page MUST NOT be done — it is a rejection in disguise, and it produces an output that looks complete and is not.

A page that is genuinely blank

A page with no ink at all MUST keep its position in the page sequence with zero elements. Its Markdown MUST consist of the single line <!-- blank page --> between the two --- separators that bound it, and its sidecar entry MUST list no items.

…end of page 1

---

<!-- blank page -->

---

Start of page 3…

Blank pages are ordinary in real documents — section breaks, duplex backs, deliberate spacers. A three-page file whose second page carries no ink and no text is not corrupt, and declaring it unrepresentable would misreport the document's length.

Neither exclusion fits:

  • Excluding a region is for a bounded exception within a page. Here there is nothing to bound.
  • Unrepresentable is for a page that cannot be represented. A blank page represents perfectly — as nothing.

The page MUST NOT be dropped — a missing page is far harder to notice than an empty one, and every later page number would shift. It MUST NOT be given an element either: an "empty" element with a box around nothing is invented. The comment says, inline and invisibly, that the page is blank on purpose, so a reader of the Markdown can tell a blank page from a lost one.

A page that prints only a notice such as "This page intentionally left blank", or only a folio or running header, has ink: it is an ordinary page whose content is that text.

✅ Sample — dense but readable

A landscape security-cover statement with sixteen columns, a Column A … Column P letter tier over two further header rows, and body text too small to read at page scale. It is slow, not impossible: every cell resolves under zoom, so nothing here is grounds to exclude a region or declare the page unrepresentable. The corner wordmark Caldrivane is an ordinary logo and is kept. The three ratio rows at the bottom merge their label across columns A–J and print no cell under Column P.

✅ Sample — a scan mark that is not content

A scanned typewritten memorandum with a small ring printed below the text, where a hole punch or a scanner roller left its mark. The ring is the bounded exception allowed above: it has no element and no box, and the rest of the page is represented, down to the folio - 63 -.

Expected Markdown

CALDRIVANE ENERGY CORP. INTEROFFICE MEMORANDUM

TO: Finance Committee FROM: R. Donovan, Treasury DATE: November 4, 2001 RE: Off-Balance-Sheet Treatment — Borvika Partners

This memorandum summarizes the accounting treatment applied to Borvika Partners, L.P., a related-party investment vehicle organized to acquire certain merchant assets that the Company did not wish to consolidate. Under the structuring in place, an outside investor holds a three-percent equity interest, which under the applicable accounting guidance is treated as sufficient independent equity at risk to keep the vehicle's assets and liabilities off the Company's consolidated balance sheet.

The Company has, however, guaranteed certain of Borvika's obligations through a series of put and forward arrangements tied to the Company's own stock. Should the Company's share price fall below the thresholds specified in those arrangements, the Company would be required to issue additional shares or make cash payments to Borvika's outside investors, which could require the vehicle's assets to be consolidated retroactively.

Management believes the three-percent threshold continues to satisfy the applicable accounting literature, and that the exposure described above, while real, is not probable of being triggered under current pricing. We recommend the Committee note this exposure for quarterly review rather than for immediate balance-sheet recognition, and that Treasury continue to monitor the share-price thresholds monthly.
